introduction.p: Limit laws allow us to calculate limits using arithmetic operations on simpler functions. We will also use algebraic simplification and inequalities when direct substitution is unavailable. Tables and graphs can suggest an answer; the calculation must justify it.

As x\to0, the denominator approaches 0, and the quotient does not approach a finite number. From the right it grows without bound; from the left it becomes negative without bound.

exercise.title: Why do nearby pieces control a nearby combination?

statement.p: If f(x) approaches L and g(x) approaches M, then their sum approaches L+M. In your own words, why is that believable from error control, and why do the limit laws refuse to run backward: a sum can have a limit even when the pieces do not?

hint.p: The error in a sum is bounded by the sum of the individual errors. Conversely, cancellation may make a sum converge even when its components have no limits.

paragraphs.title: What direct substitution can tell us
paragraphs.p: For a polynomial, or for a rational function whose denominator is nonzero at the target input, direct substitution gives the limit. More generally, substitution is valid for a function known to be continuous there.
When direct substitution gives something like
it tells us only that the direct method failed. It does not tell us the limit. The expression may have a removable hole, or it may have no finite limit.
The next examples show the difference.

exercise.title: When is plugging in legal, and when is it only a warning?

statement.p: For a polynomial, \lim_{x\to a}p(x)=p(a). For a rational function, the same substitution is legal when the denominator is not zero at a. In your own words, what does a successful substitution tell you, and what does an appearance of \frac00 refuse to tell you?

hint.p: For the polynomial and rational functions considered here, substitution gives the limit when the denominator is nonzero. In general, substitution is justified by continuity at the approach point. The form \frac00 says only that direct substitution failed; factoring, rationalizing, or another method must reveal the nearby behavior.

exercise.title: Why is \frac00 a question, not an answer?

statement.p: After canceling x-1, the function \frac{x^2-1}{x-1} agrees with x+1 near x=1, so the limit exists. Canceling in \frac{x}{x^2} produces \frac1x, which has no finite two-sided limit. In your own words, why does an indeterminate form need more work, and why is a limit allowed to ignore the missing point after rewriting?

hint.p: In a limit at a, only inputs x\ne a are relevant. Algebraic simplification may expose a limit, but the simplified expression must still be checked for unbounded or unequal one-sided behavior.

subsection.p: The squeeze principle is not a trick. It is a statement about error. If f(x) is trapped between two quantities that both get close to L, then f(x) has no room to go anywhere else.

exercise.title: How can a trapped oscillation still have a limit?

statement.p: The factor \sin(1/x) does not approach one number as x\to0, yet x^2\sin(1/x) does approach 0. In your own words, what is the squeeze idea, and why must the two outside functions approach the same target?

hint.p: If a function is trapped between two others, and those two walls close in on the same number, the trapped graph has nowhere else to go. If the walls headed toward different numbers, there would be a gap to hide in.
